slides.title: Geometric Differentiation
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter's central move: differentiation is not a single operation until the allowed variation has been chosen. A scalar parameter, a vector direction, and a multivector perturbation all produce local change, but they probe different domains. The visual deliberately puts those three channels on one stage so students can keep the syntax tied to geometric meaning.

slides.title: Choose The Domain Of Variation
slides.notes: Use this slide to slow down the notation before formulas multiply. The same limit expression is being reused, but the object \(A\) lives in the domain being probed. This is the conceptual safeguard against treating vector derivatives, parametric derivatives, and multivector derivatives as unrelated recipes. The class should see a derivative as the first-order coefficient along a declared perturbation line.

slides.title: Rotor Motion Differentiates To A Commutator
slides.notes: Present the commutator as the first major payoff of geometric algebra. A small rotor does not require separate matrix derivatives for every grade. The bivector generator tells which oriented plane is turning, and the commutator supplies the tangent velocity of the transformed object. Emphasize that the approximation is local: the quadratic remainder is evidence that the derivative captures exactly the first-order part.

slides.title: Multivector-Valued Functions Keep Their Geometry
slides.notes: Make the product rule feel familiar and new at the same time. The algebraic rule is ordinary bilinearity, but the result is not merely a pair of component derivatives. The wedge makes the derivative an oriented area-rate, so students should inspect the parallelogram and ask how changing either edge changes the blade. This prepares them for rotor and surface calculations where the value is naturally multivector-valued.

slides.title: Inversion Couples Radial And Angular Motion
slides.notes: Treat inversion as a diagnostic example because it defeats the intuition that a directional derivative should point where the input perturbation points. A small move of \(x\) decomposes into radial and angular effects after inversion. The compact formula \(-x^{-1} a x^{-1}\) is valuable because it keeps both effects in product order. Ask students to locate \(x\), \(a\), \(x^{-1}\), and the derivative arrow before reading the equation.

slides.title: The Vector Derivative Is A Basis-Summed Operator
slides.notes: The purpose here is to demystify the vector derivative by building it from directional derivatives the students already understand. In an orthonormal basis, each coordinate direction gets probed, then the basis vector is multiplied on the left before summing. That last multiplication is why the operator can return several grades. The identity and squared-length examples are familiar landmarks, but the grade-rich output is the new geometric feature.

slides.title: Gradient, Divergence, And Curl Are Grade Selections
slides.notes: Connect the GA operator to vocabulary students already know. The gradient is not a separate symbol system when the function is scalar-valued. For a vector field, the geometric product of \(\partial\) and \(F\) separates into a scalar part and a bivector part. The scalar part measures local expansion or compression, while the bivector part measures oriented circulation in coordinate planes. This is the clean GA replacement for switching between grad, div, and curl notations.

slides.title: Multivector Differentiation Follows The Object
slides.notes: This slide broadens the domain beyond vectors. Students often meet rotors, bivectors, and pseudoscalars as special objects, then unconsciously differentiate only vector coordinates. The blade atlas makes the domain explicit: the full algebra is a vector space, so every basis blade gives a legitimate perturbation direction. The linear check \(F(M)=MC\) is deliberately simple because it isolates the idea that the derivative along \(A\) is \(AC\).

slides.title: Local Linearization Is The Shared Payoff
slides.notes: Close the technical arc by returning to first-order approximation. Whether the variable is a scalar parameter, a vector, or a multivector, the derivative is the coefficient that makes \(F(X+hA)\) locally predictable. Spherical projection is a strong final picture because it visibly rejects radial motion and keeps only the tangent component. That is the chapter's habit in miniature: identify the meaningful local direction, compute its first-order effect, and then check that the remainder is second order.

slides.title: What Students Should Carry Forward
slides.notes: Use the final map as a quick oral review rather than another derivation. Ask students to place each example from the chapter on the map: rotor motion at commutator and product order, inversion at directional limit, vector derivative at grade selection, multivector functions at blade-coordinate variation, and spherical projection at local linearization. The durable habit is simple: before differentiating, name the geometric object that is allowed to move.
